classification_scheme.i: content-derived: equal content gives an equal identifier; the identifier returns whenever the content returns
classification_scheme.i*: attribute-derived (extension of i): identifier is a function of file attributes (mtime, size[, inode]) rather than content; it returns whenever those attributes return, and different content can share it
classification_scheme.ii: allocation-unique but reactivatable: each version gets a unique identifier, but a documented operation makes an older identifier current again
classification_scheme.iii: publication-fresh: every change of what is served at the name allocates a new identifier; documented restore paths allocate new identifiers; no documented path re-exposes an old identifier as current
classification_scheme.n/u: not unique: the same identifier value is re-used for different content (fails even uniqueness)
classification_scheme.n/a: feature absent (no versioning / no restore path)

quotes.quote: When you delete the current object version, you, in effect, turn the previous version into the current version of that object.
Amazon S3 supplies a new ID (88778877) and it becomes the current version of the object.
The following figure shows how deleting the current version (121212) of an object leaves the previous version (111111) as the current object.
A subsequent GET retrieves version 111111.
After you delete the current version, the previous version becomes the current version.
To undelete the object, you must delete this delete marker.
The effect of removing the delete marker is that a simple GET request will now retrieve the current version ID (121212) of the object.
To delete a delete marker with a NULL version ID, you must pass the NULL as the version ID in the DeleteObject request.
Instead, Amazon S3 inserts a delete marker in the bucket, and that marker becomes the current version of the object with a new ID.
To delete versioned objects permanently, you must use DELETE Object versionId.
If you enable versioning for a bucket, Amazon S3 automatically generates a unique version ID for the object that is being stored.
Only Amazon S3 generates version IDs, and they cannot be edited.
After you suspend versioning on a bucket, Amazon S3 automatically adds a null version ID to every subsequent object stored thereafter (using PUT, POST, or CopyObject) in that bucket.

Although the key and version ID (null) of the null version are the same before and after the PUT, the contents of the null version originally stored in the bucket are replaced by the contents of the object PUT into the bucket.

If bucket versioning is suspended, the operation removes the object that has a null versionId. If a version ID exists, Amazon S3 inserts a delete marker that becomes the current version of the object.
Retention periods and legal holds don't prevent new versions of the object from being created, or delete markers to be added on top of the object.

Permanent DELETE request – If you issued a permanent DELETE request (a request that specifies a version ID), Amazon S3 returns an Access Denied (403 Forbidden) error when you try to delete the object.
Although you can't delete a protected object version, you can still create a delete marker for that object.
Delete markers are not WORM-protected, regardless of any retention period or legal hold in place on the underlying object.
The entity tag is a hash of the object. The ETag reflects changes only to the contents of an object, not its metadata. The ETag may or may not be an MD5 digest of the object data.

Objects created by the PUT Object, POST Object, or Copy operation, or through the AWS Management Console, and are encrypted by SSE-S3 or plaintext, have ETags that are an MD5 digest of their object data.
If an object is created by either the Multipart Upload or Part Copy operation, the ETag is not an MD5 digest, regardless of the method of encryption.

An object version's generation value is unique. A new object with the same name can replace an existing object, but the new object has a different generation value.
Generation numbers might not increase for future versions, but each new version has a unique generation number.

The metageneration property has no meaning without the generation property and should be used only in conjunction with it; it's meaningless to compare metadata generations of two object versions.
In most cases, users should make no assumptions about the value used in an ETag except that it changes whenever the underlying data or metadata changes, per the specification.

When you restore an object, Cloud Storage generates a new version of the object.
